title: Build Approach Scenario Simulator: Custom Development, Template or AI Builder?
note: Spec/data file for the artifact described in ARTIFACT-BRIEF.md. This is structured content only — no HTML/JS is implemented here. The 1-5 fit scores per approach/factor are a qualitative, structural assessment of how these three build categories generally and verifiably work (auto-generation limits of AI website builders, theme/plugin architecture of visual templates, bespoke-build economics of custom development), not a measured benchmark of any specific named product, and not a Weissmann-favouring ranking. No approach is a clean sweep of 5s or 1s, and the four example scenarios below deliberately demonstrate three different winning approaches (plus one genuine close call) from the same fixed matrix, to prove to whoever implements this that the logic must never default to 'custom development' regardless of input.

scale.score: 1 (weak fit) to 5 (strong fit) per factor and approach — qualitative, not measured.
scale.weight: 0 (not important) to 3 (decisive) per factor — derived from the user's four scenario answers, never set directly by the user.

factors.label: Speed to launch
factors.description: How quickly can a working, launch-ready site realistically go live?

factors.label: Flexibility & customisation ceiling
factors.description: How high is the technical and design ceiling once the business needs something unusual?

factors.label: Differentiation from competitors
factors.description: How likely is the result to look and read as genuinely distinct, not interchangeable with similar businesses?

factors.label: Accessibility for non-technical editors
factors.description: Can someone with no development background make routine content changes themselves?

factors.label: Low ongoing maintenance burden
factors.description: How little patching, updating and technical upkeep does the business itself have to carry?

factors.label: Integration capacity
factors.description: How well can the site connect to calendars, payments, CRM or booking systems?

factors.label: Content & code ownership / portability
factors.description: How fully does the business own the result, and how easily can it be taken to a new provider?

factors.label: Technical SEO baseline
factors.description: How strong is the achievable foundation for crawlability, structured data and search visibility?

approaches.label: Fully custom development
approaches.oneLiner: The highest ceiling on control, integrations and search foundations — but the slowest launch, the highest cost and the fullest maintenance responsibility.

tradeoffs.speed: Slowest of the three by design — strategy, design and working code all have to exist before a page can go live.
tradeoffs.flexibility: No structural ceiling; anything a team can design and code, it can build, at a cost matching the ambition.
tradeoffs.differentiation: Can express a genuinely distinct identity, because nothing about the build is shared with another business.
tradeoffs.accessibility: Depends entirely on whether an editorial system was explicitly commissioned — done well it matches a template's ease, left out every edit needs a developer.
tradeoffs.maintenance: Fullest responsibility of the three: no shared platform patches things centrally, so hosting, certificates and monitoring sit with the business or its agency.
tradeoffs.integrations: Can connect to almost any system a budget allows, because the integration is simply built rather than found in a plugin store.
tradeoffs.ownership: Typically the fullest ownership of code and content, portable to a new developer if the work was documented.
tradeoffs.seo: Highest ceiling — full control over markup, speed and URL architecture — but only reached if someone actually built it properly.

approaches.label: Visual template
approaches.oneLiner: The most balanced of the three — never the worst option on any single factor, rarely the best, and usually the safest default when nothing points strongly elsewhere.

tradeoffs.speed: Choosing a theme, populating content and configuring settings typically takes days to a few weeks.
tradeoffs.flexibility: Bounded by the theme's own architecture — deep customisation is often possible, but a request outside the component library usually means a workaround.
tradeoffs.differentiation: Shares its underlying structure with every other site on the same theme, but specific content and photography can still differentiate within that shared frame.
tradeoffs.accessibility: Usually the most accessible of the three — visual, drag-and-drop or block-based editing was the point of building it that way.
tradeoffs.maintenance: Varies by setup: a self-installed content-management system needs its own ongoing updates, a standalone hosted builder patches centrally.
tradeoffs.integrations: A plugin or app ecosystem comfortably covers common cases — payments, bookings, basic CRM — but can hit a wall on anything unusual.
tradeoffs.ownership: Varies enormously: software on infrastructure the business controls is generally portable, a hosted all-in-one platform usually is not.
tradeoffs.seo: Can reach a solid, workable baseline with mature SEO-focused settings, though a heavy, poorly configured theme can undercut even a well-chosen one.

approaches.label: AI website-generation tool
approaches.oneLiner: The fastest way to a working first draft and highly approachable to edit — but typically the weakest on differentiation, integration depth and technical SEO.

tradeoffs.speed: Produces a usable first draft fastest of the three, often within minutes — though a draft and a launch-ready site are not the same claim.
tradeoffs.flexibility: Tightest of the three: most tools give limited or no direct access to underlying code, so a request outside the interface is often simply not possible.
tradeoffs.differentiation: Greatest differentiation risk of the three — drafts drawn from patterns learned across many similar businesses can end up strikingly similar without human rework.
tradeoffs.accessibility: Close to a template on ease: editing happens through the same conversational interface used to create the site, though fine-grained control can be more limited.
tradeoffs.maintenance: Provider-hosted, so the business's own patching and update load is typically low.
tradeoffs.integrations: Typically the most limited — most tools are built to produce a self-contained marketing site rather than a connected system.
tradeoffs.ownership: Least portable of the three — the generated site commonly lives inside the tool that made it, and leaving usually means rebuilding rather than migrating.
tradeoffs.seo: Typically weakest on technical depth — structured data, heading hierarchy and crawlable architecture are the unglamorous detail these tools do not yet reliably get right without review.

weightDerivation: For each factor, weight = the value (0–3) of whichever input option the user selected, per the 'governs' mapping above. 'direct' means weight = value. 'inverse' means weight = 3 − value. Each of the 8 factors is governed by exactly one of the 4 inputs (2 factors per input), so no summing or clamping is ever required — this is deliberate, so the arithmetic stays fully transparent and checkable by hand.
scoringFormula: For each of the 3 approaches: score = Σ over the 8 factors of (derived weight for that factor × that approach's 1–5 fit score for that factor). Approaches are ranked descending by this sum. Ties render as ties, never broken by a hidden rule.

exampleScenarios.label: The fast, simple launch
exampleScenarios.note: Launching this week, no differentiation need, no technical staff, staying simple. The AI builder's speed and accessibility advantage over the template is now decisive enough to win outright.

exampleScenarios.label: The steady, accessible build
exampleScenarios.note: Same non-technical, simple, low-differentiation profile as above, but with a couple of months instead of this week. That single change is enough to swing the win from the AI builder to the template, because the template's stronger accessibility and technical-SEO baseline now outweigh the AI builder's speed edge.

exampleScenarios.label: The differentiated, complex build
exampleScenarios.note: No urgency, strong differentiation need, a partner already able to handle accessibility and maintenance, and real long-run complexity. Custom development wins clearly because every high-weight factor here is exactly where it is structurally strongest.

exampleScenarios.label: The balanced, moderate case
exampleScenarios.note: Included deliberately as a close, honest call rather than a clean win: with every factor weighted moderately and evenly, custom edges out the template by only 1 point. This scenario exists to show the tool does not force a dramatic winner when the situation itself is genuinely balanced.
